variant: Cirrus Design VK-30 kit (1988-1993). Geometry is the AOPA Pilot April 1990 prototype spec block (N-1 prototype, Lycoming IO-540 290 hp) unless noted; later kit/museum figures (EAA, Wikipedia) differ slightly (span 39 ft 8 in, area 126 ft2) and are given in notes.
config: pusher (engine buried behind cabin over wing, ~6.5-ft extension driveshaft to tail-cone prop)

span.note: AOPA Pilot Apr 1990 spec block (manufacturer's calculations), prototype. EAA Museum (N33VK) and Wikipedia give 39 ft 8 in (39.67 ft): https://www.eaa.org/eaa-museum/museum-collection/aircraft-collection-folder/1991-cirrus-vk-30---n33vk

area.note: AOPA Pilot Apr 1990, wing loading 29.58 lb/ft2 at 3,550 lb (consistent). Wikipedia gives 126 ft2 / 28.6 lb/ft2 at 3,600 lb (grade R-level secondary, unsourced): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cirrus_VK-30

wing.airfoil: NASA NLF(1)-0414F root and tip (Jeff Viken, ex-NASA Langley); source: Lednicer, Incomplete Guide to Airfoil Usage https://m-selig.ae.illinois.edu/ads/aircraft.html ; Wikipedia concurs

tc_root.note: E: implied by airfoil designation NLF(1)-0414F (14% t/c); actual as-built t/c not published

tc_tip.note: E: same airfoil listed at tip

wing.winglets: no. Wing is one piece with single-piece carbon main spar and 20-ft carbon front spar; full-span Fowler flaps with sailplane-style 'cruise flaps' on their trailing edge, independently movable for roll trim (AOPA Pilot Apr 1990).

canard_or_htail.note: All-moving trim: electric trim moves entire horizontal stabilizer (AOPA Pilot Apr 1990). From photos (Wikimedia N94CM, Air Zoo N33VK-type) the stabilizer is mounted low on the aft fuselage just ahead of the prop, not a T-tail; the brief's 'cruciform' is unconfirmed. aircraftrecognitionguide.com says the VK-30 'has no ventral fin', unlike the cruciform-tailed Israviation ST50.

vtail.note: Single swept dorsal fin and rudder; dimensions not published. Height overall 10.66 ft (AOPA 1990) / 10 ft 8 in (Wikipedia).

length.note: AOPA Pilot Apr 1990; EAA Museum also 26 ft

cabin_width.note: Interior, front seat 4 ft; rear seat 4.5 ft; cabin height 4 ft; cabin length 8.5 ft (AOPA 1990 spec block; column alignment of OCR text reconstructed, verify against scan)

fuselage.note: One-piece composite fuselage shipped complete; NLF fuselage shaping. Clamshell airstair door right side. 5 seats in later kits (4 listed in 1990). Overall height 10.66 ft.

nacelles_or_booms: none; engine buried in aft fuselage over wing with side-fuselage air scoops
gear: retractable tricycle; parts adapted from Piper (PA-42 Cheyenne nose per aviacionline) and Lake LA-4 (mains) per https://aviacionline.com/kit-plane-resena-del-cirrus-vk-30-el-antecedente-del-sr-20-sr-22 (secondary, unverified). Klapmeier history says first prototype used a Cherokee nose gear modified to retract.
cooling: air-cooled; side-fuselage air scoops (reduced in size because prototype ran too cool), single electrically controlled cowl flap, large electric fan in engine bay for ground cooling (AOPA Pilot Apr 1990). V-8 auto-engine prototype #2 had radiator cooling problems and burned in flight ~1990 (Klapmeier history https://www.aircraftspruce.com/pdf/KlapmeierBrothers.pdf).

diameter.note: Hoffmann 3-blade composite/wood constant-speed on prototype. Drive: dry-fluid clutch -> 78 in x 4 in aluminium driveshaft wrapped in graphite -> 12-in steel stub shaft carrying prop thrust/bending (Molt Taylor Aerocar-derived).

rpm_cruise.note: climb setting 25 in MP / 2,500 rpm used in pilot report; cruise rpm not stated

engine.model: Prototype: Lycoming IO-540 290 hp (1990). Kits: Continental IO-550-G 300 hp typical (EAA, Wikipedia); prototype #3 Continental turbo 550; others Chevrolet V-8 auto conversion, Allison 250 turboprop (420 shp) e.g. N44VK

hp.note: IO-550 300 hp per EAA Museum; 1990 prototype 290 hp IO-540

mtow.note: AOPA 1990 manufacturer calc. EAA Museum/Wikipedia: 3,600 lb

empty.note: AOPA 1990 manufacturer calc (prototype class). EAA Museum gives 2,400 lb for N33VK-era figures. No as-built builder weights found.

fuel_usable.note: 'Fuel capacity, std 95 gal/570 lb' (total vs usable not distinguished). Secondary sources say 100 gal.

perf_points.note: AOPA Pilot Apr 1990: 'At 4,500 feet msl, the prototype cruised at a true airspeed of 205 knots at about 70-percent power and burning about 15.5 gph' (stated, not independently timed); prototype #1, ~450 h airframe
Spec block, manufacturer's calculation; 4.95 h endurance w/45-min reserve
Vso 59 KIAS (landing config), Vne 213 KIAS (prototype; 230 planned), Vfe 95, Vle 120, SL climb 1,500 fpm, takeoff roll 1,800 ft. Observed in report: ~1,000 fpm at 130 KIAS, liftoff <2,000 ft

ntsb_total.note: NTSB avall.mdb + Pre2008.mdb bulk databases downloaded 2026-10-24 (https://data.ntsb.gov/avdata), aircraft model matching /VK.?30/: 1990-08-28 CHI90DEP10 Baraboo WI (no inj); 1992-07-29 SEA92LA169 Rawlins WY (no inj); 1994-04-19 CHI94DEE01; 1996-03-22 CHI96FA116; 1996-06-03 CHI96FA185; 2007-08-27 DEN07LA148 Watrous NM; 2018-02-11 WPR18FA088. Matches Wikipedia '7 US-registered VK-30s crashed 1990-2020, 10 fatalities'. Feb 1990 forced landing in Georgia (oil line chafe) per AOPA Pilot is not in the extract. Narrative causes read from NTSB 'narratives' table.

fleet_size_for_rate.note: ~13 completed and flown (EAA); Klapmeier history says 40 kits shipped + 4 factory prototypes, 10 customer aircraft flew. 5 fatal / ~13-17 airframes = roughly 30-40% of all built lost in fatal accidents (inference).

safety.pattern: RECORD: Of 5 fatal accidents, causes per NTSB/press: (1) 1994 fuel starvation from builder fuel-system modification; (2) 1996 Overmyer, Allison-turbine VK-30 N44VK, failed to recover from aft-CG spin during stall testing of new wings - NTSB cited 'inadequate handling/performance design capabilities' and lack of antispin/deep-stall recovery devices; (3) 1996 in-flight flutter/breakup from cruise-flap failure (incomplete bond cure, wrong hinge material, bad welding); (4) 2007 N60GE forced landing gone wrong after a ruptured pressurized oil line (smoke trailing); (5) 2018 N52TH in-flight driveshaft fracture (coupling nuts backed off), flailing shaft knocked off the tail fairing -> loss of control, 4 killed. Non-fatal: 1990 fuel exhaustion (inop totalizer), 1992 crosswind loss of control. Earlier: 1990 prototype engine seizure from chafed long prop-governor oil line (forced landing, no injuries); prototype #2 (V-8) in-flight fire. In 1996 Cirrus recommended grounding all VK-30s pending new wings after finding potential wing-material defects (AOPA Pilot May 1996). INFERENCE: Three of five fatal accidents clearly (driveshaft, cruise flap, aft-CG spin) and possibly a fourth (2007 oil line, if it was the long governor line) and both prototype incidents trace to configuration-specific complexity (long driveshaft/couplings, long oil line, cruise-flap mechanism, buried-engine systems) or to aft-CG departure behaviour typical of aft-engine layouts; the rest is builder quality. A revival must design out the shaft/coupling and flap complexity and prove spin/deep-stall recovery.
notable: 1996-03-22 - Duluth MN - N44VK, 1 fatal (Robert Overmyer) - aft-CG spin during stall test, non-recovery; NTSB CHI96FA116 - https://www.aopa.org/news-and-media/all-news/1996/may/pilot/pilot-briefing-(5) ; https://aviation-safety.net/wikibase/41280
1994-04-19 - Lake in the Hills IL - N108P, 2 fatal - fuel starvation from fuel-system modification; NTSB CHI94DEE01 - https://aviation-safety.net/wikibase/39452

1996-06-03 - Lapeer MI - N7033G, 1 fatal - right-wing flutter after cruise-flap bracket failure (incomplete bond cure, improper hinge material, improper welding of pushrod end caps); NTSB CHI96FA185 - https://aviation-safety.net/wikibase/41249

2007-08-27 - Watrous NM - N60GE, 2 fatal - pilot failed to maintain control in forced landing (hard landing, nose-up ~11-12 deg, 3 prop-strike marks) after engine trouble; contributing: ruptured pressurized oil line, smoke trailing; NTSB DEN07LA148 (NTSB avall narrative)

2018-02-11 - Agua Dulce CA - N52TH, 4 fatal - NTSB: driveshaft fracture (overstress, rotational bending) after under-torqued nuts on elastomeric couplings backed off; separated shaft end struck and detached the horizontal [tail] fairing, leading to loss of control; contributing: inadequate maintenance (retorque 5.1 h earlier); NTSB WPR18FA088 - https://data.ntsb.gov/carol-repgen/api/Aviation/ReportMain/GenerateNewestReport/96726/pdf ; https://aviation-safety.net/wikibase/206020
1990-08-28 - Baraboo WI - no injuries - fuel exhaustion, misjudged fuel, inoperative fuel totalizer factor; NTSB CHI90DEP10
1992-07-29 - Rawlins WY - no injuries - loss of control in crosswind/gusts; NTSB SEA92LA169

why_died_detail: Kit sales were weak (8 sold + 16 deposits by Apr 1990; ~40 kits total); build complexity (2,000 h estimate, systems-heavy pusher with driveshaft, Fowler + cruise flaps) and high kit price ($42,500 in 1990). Klapmeiers concluded 'we failed as kitmakers... the only way to go was Part 23' and pivoted to the conventional tractor SR20; they then tried to buy back outstanding kits and recovered about three-quarters (Klapmeier history, aircraftspruce PDF). 1996 wing-material defect led Cirrus to recommend grounding pending new wings. A turbine derivative evolved into the Israviation/Cirrus ST50 (single proof-of-concept built in Israel). Revival relevance: the NLF pusher concept itself gave 205-211 kt on 290 hp; the failures were in drivetrain/flap systems, aft-CG spin recovery and kit complexity.
rights_hints: Plane & Pilot says the Klapmeiers 'sold the rights to an Israeli company for certification' which never happened (https://planeandpilotmag.com/cirrus-design-vk30/) - possibly conflated with the Israviation ST50 turbine derivative (https://aircraftrecognitionguide.com/israviation-st50). Cirrus bought back ~3/4 of outstanding kits (aircraftspruce Klapmeier PDF). Current holder of VK-30 molds/tooling/design data not found; presumably Cirrus Design (now Cirrus Aircraft, owned by AVIC/CAIGA since 2011) unless transferred. Surviving airframes: N33VK at EAA Museum (donated 2005), N94CM displayed Florida Air Museum, one at Air Zoo; ~4 FAA-registered in 2018 (Wikipedia).
